syllabus.clause: colour invariants as an encoding of 2-3-4 trees, at most three rotations per update and O(1) amortized recolourings

at.step: Every node is red or black, the root is black, a red node never has a red child, and every path down to empty space passes through the same number of black nodes.
A black node and its red children aren't really separate nodes — they're one node of a 2-3-4 tree, wearing a disguise.
The climb can be as tall as the tree. The rotation at the bottom of it never is.

items.item: Recolouring is tried first because it is cheaper than a rotation and often sufficient by itself; a rotation is reached for only in the specific cases recolouring alone cannot resolve.

at.step: Recolouring fixes most violations by itself. When it can't, one rotation finishes the job — the same move last topic defined, now firing for a reason.

items.item: The 2-3-4 correspondence is not a separate fact about red-black trees to memorize alongside the colour invariant — the colour invariant is that correspondence, restated in binary-tree terms.

items.item: The rotation bound (two for insert, three for delete) is not obvious from the recolouring loop's own unbounded climb — the two facts (climb length, rotation count) are independent, and the second is what actually matters for cost.

items.item: The reason the scheme stays cheap is specifically that the expensive-looking part (the recolouring climb) is not the part that is bounded, and the bounded part (rotations) is not the part that looks expensive.

items.item: The height bound is a direct consequence of the 2-3-4 correspondence (each 2-3-4 node expands into at most two tree levels), not a separately-proven fact about red-black trees specifically.

at.step: The 2-3-4 correspondence is what does the real work: every 2-3-4 node expands into at most two tree levels, so a red-black tree's height can never run away the way an unbalanced BST's did.
